title: Who is at high risk from climate hazards? A new map to explore exposure and vulnerability
gist: The World Bank's PARCH map combines climate-hazard exposure with household vulnerability: over 4.5 billion people will likely face a major flood, drought, heatwave or cyclone in their lifetime, and about 1.2 billion (1.5 billion extrapolated) are at high risk. The share at high risk fell from one in three to one in five since 2010.

insights.claim: Under current climate conditions more than half of the world's population, over 4.5 billion people, will likely face at least one major flood, drought, heatwave or cyclone in their lifetime.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Climate hazard exposure is majority-global, so physical risk is not a niche exposure.

insights.claim: About 1.2 billion people in countries with available data are at high risk from climate hazards, rising to 1.5 billion (nearly one in five) when extrapolated to the global population.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: The Bank now has an official headline metric for climate-vulnerable people that can anchor adaptation financing.

insights.claim: The PARCH map separates exposure (living where a damaging hazard is sufficiently likely, e.g. a 1 percent annual chance of floods above 0.5 meters or a Category 2+ cyclone) from vulnerability, and counts people who are both as at risk.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Exposure alone overstates risk; combine hazard and vulnerability when assessing populations.
insights.locator: Two questions: who is exposed, and who is vulnerable?

insights.claim: Vulnerability is measured across seven areas using basic minimum thresholds such as living below the US$3.00-a-day poverty line, no one with completed primary school, and lacking a bank or mobile money account, electricity or safe drinking water.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: The vulnerability definition is deliberately minimal, targeting those least able to recover.
insights.locator: Two questions: who is exposed, and who is vulnerable?

insights.claim: The World Bank Group Scorecard indicator uses the broadest setting, counting people exposed to any hazard and vulnerable in any area.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: The headline number is the upper-bound definition, so narrower selections yield smaller figures.

insights.claim: Exposure is highest in South and East Asia but vulnerability there is lower thanks to broader social protection and financial services, whereas in Sub-Saharan Africa 90 percent of people are highly vulnerable on at least one dimension so nearly everyone exposed is at risk.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Sub-Saharan Africa is the region where hazard shocks translate most directly into losses and aid needs.

insights.claim: Globally more people are exposed to heatwaves than any other hazard, while most rural people face agricultural drought, often while vulnerable in more than one way.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Rural agricultural drought exposure points to food-security and crop-income risk.

insights.claim: The share of people at high risk fell from about one in three to one in five since 2010, driven largely by declining socioeconomic vulnerability, while exposure stayed broadly similar as a share of population.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Poverty reduction and service access, not lower hazard, have cut climate risk, so development progress is a climate adaptation lever.

insights.claim: The number of people exposed to climate hazards grew by 461 million since 2010, partly reflecting population growth.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Absolute exposure keeps rising even as the at-risk share falls.

insights.claim: The map counts only people directly in a hazard's path, excludes countries lacking recent household surveys, and the latest numbers trail the present by a few years.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Treat figures as a lower-bound, lagged measure.
insights.locator: Keep in mind that the map counts people
